cards.title: Finite and non-finite clauses
rule: A **finite clause** has a verb that shows tense and agrees with a subject: *She **faces** many challenges.* *Because he **was** ill, ...*

A **non-finite clause** has no tense; its verb is a **to-infinitive**, an **-ing participle** or a **past participle**: ***To succeed**, you must work hard.* ***Facing** many problems, she never gave up.* ***Given** enough time, we can solve it.*
The subject of a participle clause must be the same as the main clause subject: *Walking home, **I** saw an accident* (I was walking).

Walking to school, the rain started.

cards.problem: Which of the following sentences exhibits the correct English word order (S-V-O)?

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object (S-V-O) pattern.
The subject is 'The security guard', the verb is 'locked', and the direct object is 'the main gate'.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Option A and Option C place the verb ('locked') at the end of the clause, which is an S-O-V pattern typical of Tigrinya grammar (ሓላው ሰላም ማዕጾ ዓጸዎ) and represents a common translation from Tigrinya error.

cards.answer: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which sentence is missing a linking verb (is/am/are/was/were)?

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires a linking verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the word that describes the subject.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** In Option C, the linking verb 'is' is completely missing.

In Tigrinya, the linking verb can sometimes be omitted or structurally merged, leading students to translate "ሓወይ ኣብቲ ዓዲ ትጉህ ሓረስታይ [እዩ]" directly as "My brother a hardworking farmer..." without including the linking verb 'is'.

cards.answer: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence that correctly manages sentence boundaries without creating a comma splice.

options.A: The rain was heavy, we decided to stay indoors.
options.B: The rain was heavy we decided to stay indoors.
options.C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.
options.D: Because the rain was heavy, so we decided to stay indoors.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined with only a comma. Option A is a comma splice. Option B is a run-on sentence. Option C uses a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb ('therefore'), which is structurally perfect.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option D is a double-conjunction error ('Because... so...'). Tigrinya speakers often use both because they translate word endings like "ስለዝ-... ስለዚ..." directly into English. Option C correctly separates the clauses.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ክልተ ናጻ ዝኾኑ ምሉእ ሓሳባት (independent clauses) ብኮማ ጥራይ ከተኣሳሰሩ ኣይኽእሉን እዮም (እዚ Comma Splice ይበሃል)። ኣብ Option C ዝተጠቐስናሉ ሰሚኮለን (;) ንሰንሰለት ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብግቡእ ይዓጽዎ። Option D ድማ 'Because' ን 'so' ን ብሓባር ብምጥቃም ዝተገብረ ልሙድ ናይ ትርጉም ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Complete the sentence with the correct word order: 'The school principal ________.'

options.A: yesterday welcomed the new students warmly
options.B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday
options.C: welcomed yesterday warmly the new students
options.D: the new students welcomed warmly yesterday

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
English adverbs of manner ('warmly') usually precede the main verb or follow the object. Adverbs of time ('yesterday') belong at the end of the sentence. The correct structure is: Subject ('The school principal') + Adverb of Manner ('warmly') + Verb ('welcomed') + Object ('the new students') + Adverb of Time ('yesterday').

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option D shows S-O-V word order. Option A places the time adverb ('yesterday') between the subject and the verb, which is acceptable in Tigrinya but highly irregular and awkward in English unless formatted as a fronted adverbial.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ናይ ግዜ ተወሳኺ ሓበሬታ (Adverb of Time - 'yesterday') ወትሩ ኣብ መወዳእታ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ክስራዕ ከሎ፡ ናይ ኣገባብ ተወሳኺ ሓበሬታ (Adverb of Manner - 'warmly') ድማ ቅድሚ እቲ ዋና ግሲ ይመጽእ። Option B ነዚ ናይ S-V-O ስርዓት ብትኽክል ዝሓለወ እዩ።

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A finite clause has a verb showing tense with a subject.

**Step 2:** "the road was closed" has a subject and past tense.

**Step 3:** The others are to-infinitive, perfect participle and past participle clauses.

cards.title: Break down a long sentence
cards.problem: Find the main subject, main verb and the main message of: "The young engineer, who had grown up in a village without electricity and had studied by candlelight for years, designed a solar lamp that now lights thousands of homes."

steps.text: **Step 1: Remove the relative clause.** Cut "who had grown up in a village without electricity and had studied by candlelight for years" (it only describes the engineer).
**Step 2: Find the core.** "The young engineer designed a solar lamp." Subject: the young engineer; main verb: designed.
**Step 3: Look at what is left.** "that now lights thousands of homes" describes the lamp.
**Step 4: State the message.** An engineer from a poor village invented a solar lamp that is now widely used.

cards.answer: Subject: the young engineer; main verb: designed; message: he invented a solar lamp now used in thousands of homes.

cards.title: Subordination
rule: A **subordinate clause** cannot stand alone; it depends on a main clause. It starts with a **subordinator**: time (*when, while, after, before, until*), reason (*because, since, as*), contrast (*although, though, whereas*), condition (*if, unless*), purpose (*so that*), relative (*who, which, that*).
Comma rule: when the subordinate clause comes **first**, use a comma: ***Although the novel is long,** it is exciting.*

Although he was poor. He was happy.

cards.problem: The manager rejected the proposal because he felt that ________ details were provided to support the budget.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The blank modifies the noun 'details'. 'Details' is a plural countable noun (indicated by the '-s' ending).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Uncountable quantifiers like 'little' and 'a little' cannot modify plural countable nouns. 'Too few' is the correct quantifier for countable nouns in a negative context.
Tigrinya speakers often conflate 'few' and 'little' as both translate to 'ውሑድ' or 'ቅሩብ'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Although the construction project has been delayed, ________ progress has been made this week.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Progress' is an uncountable noun in English. It cannot be pluralized and cannot pair with countable quantifiers.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
'A few' and 'many' are strictly countable. 'Few' is also countable. 'Some' can modify both countable and uncountable nouns, making it the only grammatically viable option here.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Progress' (ዕብየት/ምስጓም) ዘይቝጸር ስም (uncountable noun) እዩ። 'Many' ን 'a few' ን ንዝቝጸሩ ስማት ጥራይ ስለ ዝኾኑ ምስ 'progress' ክኸዱ ኣይኽእሉን። 'Some' ግን ምስ ክልቲኦም ስለ ዝኸይድ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Police' is a collective noun that is grammatically plural and always takes a plural verb.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular).
The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense (has/have + V3).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased'.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** This is a direct question in the past simple tense.
Questions require subject-auxiliary inversion: Wh-word + auxiliary (didn't) + Subject (you) + base verb (complete).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The rare African manuscript ________ from the national archives before the guards noticed the broken window.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The sentence describes two past events: the manuscript being stolen and the guards noticing the broken window. The theft happened before the guards noticed it, requiring the past perfect passive voice (had been + V3).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option A ('was stolen') is simple past passive. While grammatically correct in isolation, it does not correctly sequence the two past actions. Option D ('has been stolen') is present perfect, which cannot be paired with the simple past past clause ('before the guards noticed').

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**

cards.title: Adverbs of frequency
rule: From most to least: **always, usually, often, sometimes, seldom/rarely, hardly ever, never**.
Position: **before** the main verb (*I **often** use a computer*) but **after** be (*She is **always** late*) and after the first auxiliary (*I have **never** seen it*).
**seldom, rarely, hardly ever, never** already have a negative meaning, so do NOT add *not*: *I **hardly ever** watch TV* (not *I don’t hardly ever*).

units.title: Expectations
units.intro: Grammar: idiomatic expressions and inversion (So do I, Neither do I, Not only ... but also).

cards.title: Idiomatic expressions
rule: An **idiom** is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words: *break the ice* = start a conversation; *a piece of cake* = very easy; *once in a blue moon* = very rarely; *hit the books* = study hard; *under the weather* = slightly ill.
Learn idioms as whole units and from context; don’t translate word by word.

examples.text: The test was a piece of cake.
He is under the weather (= standing outside in the rain).
examples.fix: Under the weather means slightly ill.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: One of the most challenging obstacles facing high school graduates ________ the rising cost of higher education.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The subject of the sentence is 'One' (singular) in the pattern One of + Plural Noun + Singular Verb.
The plural noun phrase 'the most challenging obstacles' is part of a prepositional phrase modifying the subject.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often match the verb to the plural noun 'obstacles' which is closest to the verb slot, leading them to choose 'are'.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The board of directors, despite having conflicting opinions on the new expansion policy, ________ finally agreed on the budget.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The subject is 'The board' (singular collective noun).
The phrase 'of directors' and the parenthetical clause 'despite having conflicting opinions...' are intervening elements that do not change the subject's singular number.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students are often distracted by the plural nouns 'directors' and 'opinions' and select the plural auxiliary 'have'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Neither the regional program coordinator nor the senior researchers ________ present at the emergency project meeting yesterday.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The compound subject is connected by the correlative conjunction 'Neither... nor'. The proximity rule applies, meaning the verb agrees with the closer subject, 'the senior researchers' (plural).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students may focus on 'the coordinator' (singular) and choose 'was' (Option A). The past time marker 'yesterday' eliminates present auxiliaries 'is' and 'are', leaving 'were' (Option B) as the correct choice.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'Neither... nor' ክእሰር ከሎ፡ እቲ ግሲ ምስቲ ናብኡ ዝቐረበ ባእታ ይሰማማዕ (Proximity Rule)። እቲ ዝቐረበ ባእታ 'the senior researchers' (ብዙሕ) ስለ ዝኾነን እቲ ግዜ ድማ 'yesterday' (ትማሊ) ስለ ዝኾነን፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'were' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The local police ________ currently searching the forest area for the prisoners who escaped from the regional jail.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Police' is a collective noun that is always plural in English and must be paired with plural verbs.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Because 'police' does not end in '-s', students often assume it is singular and choose 'is' (Option A) or 'was' (Option C). The time marker 'currently' indicates present tense, which makes 'are' (Option B) correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ብቅርጹ ነጸላ ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ወግዒ ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) እዩ። 'currently' (ኣብዚ እዋን) ዝብል ቃል ድማ ህልው እዋን ስለ ዝሕብር፡ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What does "once in a blue moon" mean?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A "blue moon" is a rare event, so the idiom means very rarely.

**Step 2:** It has nothing to do with the colour of the moon.

**Step 3:** Example: He visits us once in a blue moon.

**Tip:** Idioms have meanings that differ from their separate words. After negative adverbs (never, rarely, not only, hardly) at the start, invert the subject and auxiliary.

cards.title: Inversion
rule: **So / Neither + auxiliary + subject** to agree: *I like music. — **So do I**.* *I can’t swim. — **Neither can I**.* Use the same auxiliary as the first sentence (do/does/did for simple tenses).

After negative words at the start (*Not only, Never, Seldom, Hardly, Rarely*) put the **auxiliary before the subject**: ***Not only did he** pass, **but** he **also** won a prize.* ***Never have I** seen such a crowd.*

examples.text: She passed and so did her brother.
Not only he passed but also...
examples.fix: Not only did he pass, but he also...

examples.text: Seldom do we see snow here.

cards.pattern: So/Neither + aux + S  ·  Not only + aux + S + V, but ... also

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Not only he passed but also..."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **So / Neither + auxiliary + subject** to agree: *I like music. — **So do I**.* *I can’t swim. — **Neither can I**.* Use the same auxiliary as the first sentence (do/does/did for simple tenses).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Not only he passed but also..." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Not only did he pass, but he also..."

**Check:** After negative words at the start (*Not only, Never, Seldom, Hardly, Rarely*) put the **auxiliary before the subject**: ***Not only did he** pass, **but** he **also** won a prize.* ***Never have I** seen such a crowd.*
